title: Policy-driven multi-tenant routing lab
content:
Overview:
This hands-on lab demonstrates how to implement policy-driven routing for a multi-tenant Redwood deployment. Attendees will walk through:
- defining per-tenant policies (latency-first, cost-first, reliability-first),
- wiring policies into the request router,
- simulating load and failure modes, and
- observing behavior in the Console (per-route metrics and fallback events).

Why this matters:
Many customers run multiple product lines/tenants on a single inference fabric. Policy-driven routing lets platform teams guarantee tenant-level SLAs and unit economics without siloing capacity per tenant. This lab is practical: minimal infra, reproducible, and focused on debugging common edge cases.

Goals (30–45m):
- Create three synthetic tenants with distinct routing policies.
- Route identical API calls to different model variants based on policy.
- Force a model outage and validate automatic fallback behavior.
- Tune routing weights and observe cost/latency tradeoffs.

Prereqs (put in attendee checklist):
- Redwood CLI installed and authenticated (redwood-cli v0.48+).
- Local Docker (for the simple load generator) or remote runner.
- Access to a sandbox Redwood account with two model variants: small-v1 (cheap) and medium-v2 (balanced).
- Console access to view per-route metrics.

Quick architecture (whiteboard):
- Ingress -> Policy Router -> Model Pool (small-v1, medium-v2)
- Router evaluates tenant metadata + request headers + runtime metrics -> selects endpoint or fallback
- Observability: per-tenant traces, fallback counter, token cost meter

Lab steps (detailed):
1) Create tenants and sample policies (5m)
- TenantA: latency-first (prefer medium-v2, allow small-v1 only if medium overloaded)
- TenantB: cost-first (prefer small-v1 unless latency >300ms)
- TenantC: reliability-first (always prefer medium-v2, automatic region fallback on errors)

Sample policy YAML (paste into a new routing config):

policy_name: tenantB-cost-first
priority_rules:
  - when: "tenant == 'TenantB'"
    prefer: small-v1
    failover:
      - model: medium-v2
        condition: "latency > 300ms"
    score_weights:
      latency: 0.3
      cost: 0.7

Notes: this is intentionally simple YAML used by the router to rank endpoints. In the real platform the router uses more signals (sequence length distribution, kv-cache hit rate).

2) Upload routing config and enable the policy in the sandbox project (CLI) (5m)
- redwood routing apply --file tenantB-cost-first.yaml --project sandbox-poc
- CLI will return a routing config ID (save it for validation)

3) Bind tenants to policies (3m)
- redwood tenant create TenantB --policy tenantB-cost-first --project sandbox-poc

4) Deploy two model variants to the model pool (10m)
- small-v1: 6GB quantized model, 8 tps baseline
- medium-v2: 16GB float16 model, 20 tps baseline
- Commands (example):
  - redwood model upload --name small-v1 --path s3://redwood-demo-models/small-v1 --project sandbox-poc
  - redwood model upload --name medium-v2 --path s3://redwood-demo-models/medium-v2 --project sandbox-poc
  - redwood model allocate --model small-v1 --pool shared-pool --replicas 2
  - redwood model allocate --model medium-v2 --pool shared-pool --replicas 1

5) Quick sanity test (3m)
- Call the hosted API with tenant header and look at the route decision in the response metadata.
- Example curl: 
  curl -s -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate \ 
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_KEY" \ 
    -H "X-Redwood-Tenant: TenantB" \ 
    -d '{"model":"policy-router","input":"say hi"}'
- Expectation: response includes route: small-v1 or medium-v2 depending on runtime scoring.

6) Load test and observe behavior (15m)
- Use the included load-gen script (docker) to generate steady qps per tenant: 10 qps for TenantA, 8 qps for TenantB, 12 qps for TenantC.
- Command: docker run --rm -e REDWOOD_KEY=$REDWOOD_KEY redwood/load-gen:policy-router --tenants config/tenants.json --qps 30 --duration 600
- Observe Console: per-tenant latency, fallback count, cost per token.
- Look for TenantB favoring small-v1 under normal load.

7) Failure injection: simulate medium-v2 outage (10m)
- In Console or via CLI mark medium-v2 as degraded: redwood model set-state --model medium-v2 --state degraded --project sandbox-poc
- Expected: TenantA (latency-first) should route to medium-v2 until degraded, then fallback to small-v1 with a spike in latency. TenantC (reliability-first) should attempt regional fallback path (if configured). TenantB (cost-first) may already be on small-v1; observe little change.
- Check buckets: fallback_counter, failover_latency, token_cost metrics.

8) Tune weights and re-evaluate (10m)
- Edit the policy to increase cost weight for TenantA to favor cheaper model when cost overrun threshold exceeded.
- Apply and run short load spike to validate behavior.

Sample runtime debug tips (notes to self):
- If router logs show "no eligible endpoints" check model allocation and region tags. Often caused by model tag mismatch (e.g., "cpu-only" vs expected "gpu").
- Fallbacks are recorded in the "router.events.fallback" metric. Use Console filter by tenant to debug.
- If token cost isn’t matching expected, inspect request metadata: streaming vs non-streaming tokens are billed differently in our billing pipeline.

Mini-code snippets (Python) — show routing header and observe meta: 

import requests
import os

API = 'https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate'
KEY = os.environ.get('REDWOOD_KEY')

headers = {
  'Authorization': f'Bearer {KEY}',
  'X-Redwood-Tenant': 'TenantB',
  'Content-Type': 'application/json'
}
data = {
  'model': 'policy-router',
  'input': 'Write a micro docstring for the router decision function',
  'max_tokens': 64
}
resp = requests.post(API, headers=headers, json=data)
print(resp.json())

Troubleshooting checklist (fast):
- Router responding 500: check policy syntax (YAML parser errors) and verify config ID in routing table.
- Unexpected routing to medium-v2: ensure latency thresholds evaluated against 95th percentile, not mean. Misunderstanding common.
- Console shows high cold-start latency: confirm warmup policy + keepalive replicas.

Exercise variants / extensions (optional):
- Canary routing: add a rollout percentage for a new experimental model and observe metrics for a small tenant subset.
- Cost backpressure: configure router to reject requests (429) when per-tenant spend rate exceeds monthly quota.
- Region-aware routing: force TenantC to run in eu-west-1 and validate cross-region fallback.

Post-lab artifacts to create:
- Workshop slide deck: 10 slides (overview + steps + metrics screenshots)
- Short recording: 8–10 minutes of the failure injection demonstration
- Reference repo: small scripts + sample YAMLs (link to PR provided above).

Open questions / TODOs (internal):
- Do we expose request-level policy debug as a flag in the hosted API? (Priya to investigate)
- Add simulated cost meter to load-gen so teams can practice cost-based routing. (Tomas assigned)

Notes to facilitator: keep pace tight, assume attendees comfortable with CLI and basic Redwood concepts. Focus debugging time on the failure injection and Console observations — that's the part product teams find most convincing.

Appendix: sample tenants.json for load-gen
[
  {"tenant": "TenantA", "qps": 10},
  {"tenant": "TenantB", "qps": 8},
  {"tenant": "TenantC", "qps": 12}
]

-- end of lab --
